paper_title: Assessing the CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models: A Case Study of GPT-6 Astra

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent advances in general-purpose AI models and agentic systems have enabled them to perform some CAD tasks. A systematic assessment is now needed to establish what these systems can accomplish and how well their outputs meet engineering requirements. This paper presents an empirical study of GPT-6 Astra, a SOTA general-purpose AI model, across four basic CAD tasks: model understanding, generation, editing, and evaluation. We design test cases spanning different levels of complexity and engineering requirements. The results show that GPT-6 Astra can support multiple stages of CAD workflows, with successful outcomes in cases involving nontrivial geometric complexity. This suggests that general-purpose AI is beginning to offer practical value in almost all steps in CAD workflow. However, gaps remain between generating visually plausible geometry and producing valid, functional, and editable CAD models. Recurring errors in freeform geometry, parameter dependencies, and mating relationships between parts limit engineering usefulness. Agentic iterative refinement can improve results but does not consistently resolve critical errors; long completion times further constrain practical use.

sections.content: 1 Assessing the CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models: Case Study of GPT-6 Astra Qiang Zou*, Jiajun Shen, Zhijie Yang, Yuhao Wang, Shitianyi Leng, Dongshuo Yin State Key Laboratory of CAD&CG, Zhejiang University, China Abstract Recent advances in general-purpose AI models and agentic systems have enabled them to perform some CAD tasks. systematic assessment is now needed to establish what these systems can accomplish and how well their outputs meet engineering requirements. KeywordsComputer-aided design, general-purpose artificial intelligence, agentic systems, CAD evaluation, solid modeling, parametric feature modeling I. Introduction Recent advances in foundation models, code generation, and tool use have enabled general-purpose AI systems to perform growing range of computer-aided design (CAD) tasks. For example, they can interpret design inputs, execute modeling commands, inspect geometry, and revise outputs using feedback [13]. Systematic assessment is therefore needed to establish which CAD tasks these systems can support, whether their outputs meet engineering requirements, and where specialized CAD methods remain necessary. CAD models encode design intent and support subsequent editing, analysis, and manufacturing. Their quality therefore depends on geometric accuracy, solid validity, parametric editability, and conformance to functional and process requirements [4, 5]. model may reproduce parts visible appearance well while containing disconnected passages or incompatible assembly interfaces. It may also match the initial geometry yet lose required features when dimension changes. These failures highlight the need to assess the accuracy, validity, usability, and behavior under modification of AIgenerated CAD models. Relevant evaluation studies exist. Picard et al. [6] investigated drawing interpretation, CAD generation, and machining feature recognition, although their tests used an oversimplified case: block with blind hole. More recent benchmarks assess CAD generation, reconstruction and editing [711]. CADWorld evaluates agents operating FreeCAD through its graphical interface [12]. These studies address different subsets of CAD work, and most of their test cases are synthetically generated and differ substantially from those encountered in engineering practice. This paper presents the first systematic, in-depth empirical assessment of general-purpose AI capabilities covering the very four basic CAD tasks of model understanding, generation, editing, and autonomous evaluation [13]. The full report can be found in the Appendix. Specifically, we use GPT-6 Astra as case study, conducting six kinds of CAD tests: part classification, machining feature recognition, CAD generation from engineering drawings, text, and rendered images, and parametric reconstruction from boundary representation (B-rep) models. The cases span different levels of complexity and engineering requirements. All cases are drawn from real engineering practice. The evaluation results suggest emerging practical value for AI in design intent understanding in conceptual design and initial geometric modeling for detailed design. AI can now effectively interpret design intent from text and images, construct geometry, build parts and assemblies, and develop designs from functional requirements. However, recurring errors in freeform geometry, parameter dependencies, and mating relationships between parts limit the usefulness of the outputs. Refinement corrects some defects but leaves others unresolved or exacerbates other geometric errors; moreover, long completion times impose further practical constraint. Professional verification remains necessary in AI+CAD. * Corresponding author. Qiangzou@cad.zju.edu.cn 2 The main contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. An assessment design that systematically covers four basic CAD tasks through six kinds of tests, with cases selected from real engineering practice, and spanning different levels of geometric complexity and engineering requirements. 2. An empirical study that systematically assesses geometric accuracy, solid validity, parametric editability, and compliance with functional requirements. 3. An analysis of recurring failures in AI+CAD, which identifies the systems practical capabilities and remaining engineering limitations. II. Assessment Design This section provides high-level overview of the assessment objectives, design rationale, and experimental settings. Detailed descriptions are available in the full evaluation report in the Appendix: Chapter 1 presents the overall framework and settings, while the first sections of Chapters 27 describes the corresponding task and evaluation criteria in each tested CAD tasks. A. Assessment objectives and design rationale The objective of this study is to determine whether todays AI-generated CAD models are suitable for engineering use. This requires examining whether general-purpose AI can understand mechanical structures, develop designs autonomously from requirements, and repeatedly evaluate and revise its work as engineers do. These questions motivate joint assessment of four basic CAD tasks: understanding, generation, editing, and evaluation. Understanding parts and features involves interpreting geometric structure and engineering meaning [14, 15], while generation expresses design in CAD representation [16]. Editing tests whether the model preserves intended relationships when design parameters change [5]. Evaluation supports these activities through checking and iterative refinement. Together, these tasks provide basis for assessing both the creation of CAD models and their suitability for subsequent use. Also, they can be easily decomposed into the six kinds of CAD tests as shown in Table I, which can be connected to low-level detailed CAD workflow. Engineering suitability depends on both the quality of the initial model and its behavior during subsequent modification. CAD model must represent the intended geometry and function, maintain solid validity, and preserve required relationships as design parameters change. We therefore assess geometric accuracy, solid validity, functional adequacy, and parametric editability separately. We also examine the agents checking and refinement process to determine whether successive revisions correct defects, preserve requirements already satisfied, and improve model quality. Together, these assessments establish what the system can accomplish and how reliably its outputs can support engineering design. TABLE Main test sets and task-specific sources of complexity. B. Case design principles Cases are drawn from engineering practice and selected to examine how geometric complexity and interactions among features, components, and parameters affect engineering usefulness. Case selection follows the capability being assessed, with distinct design considerations for understanding, generation, editing, and iteration/evaluation. For understanding, cases test interpretation at both the part and feature levels. Overall geometry must support identification of the part, while local geometry must support recognition of machining features and their relationships. Intersecting features, nested structures, and ambiguous boundaries are included to probe interpretation beyond isolated, readily recognizable shapes. For generation, cases vary both the input representation and the extent to which the design is specified. Drawings, rendered images, and text impose different interpretation demands, while functional requirements leave design decisions to the system. Internal structures and mating interfaces introduce requirements that cannot be assessed from external appearance alone. For editing, cases exercise dependencies among features and components, testing whether reconstructed parametric models preserve required geometry and relationships when dimensions change. Initial geometric agreement and subsequent editability are therefore assessed separately. For evaluation, it is examined throughout the tests by relating the agents own checking and refinement to independently verified output quality. This establishes whether revisions correct defects, preserve requirements already satisfied, or introduce new errors. Complexity is defined within each task according to the interpretation demands, feature interactions, and parameter dependencies involved. These levels support comparisons within tasks, while cross-task analysis examines recurring difficulties in meeting engineering requirements. Table summarizes the six test sets and their principal complexity factors, and Figure 1 shows representative cases. For all the details of the tested cases, please refer to the first sections of Chapters 27 in the full report of the Appendix. Figure 1. Representative cases from the six kinds of CAD tests. 4 C. C. Experimental setting and verification All tests use GPT-6 Astra at the MAX reasoning setting in the ChatGPT client, with Codex mode connected to Linux server. Each run uses an independent conversation with the memoryless working mode. The agent can read the supplied files, execute code, configure its working environment, and use available tools subject to the task instructions. Web search is enabled in the main tests and disabled in selected supplementary runs. Within single conversational turn, the agent can carry out multiple cycles of execution, checking, and revision. For all the details of the setup, please refer to Table 1-2 in Appendix. Output quality is verified separately from the agents own assessment, using geometric comparisons, solid-validity checks, and inspection against task-specific engineering requirements as appropriate. For parametric reconstructions that pass the initial solid-validity checks, prescribed manual dimension changes test whether the model rebuilds correctly and preserves the required relationships. These tests measure the editability of the generated model. Recorded completion times cover the full task execution, including environment setup, tool use, and autonomous refinement. The full evaluation report in the Appendix provides the complete task instructions, case descriptions, task-specific procedures and verification criteria, and detailed results. III. Results Table II summarizes the main tests. Successful recognition or generation often coexists with defects found by further checks. Supplementary runs are reported within each task and excluded from the main-test counts. Table III summarizes the working time for individual tests. TABLE II Results for the main tests. Part classification This task evaluates whether GPT-6 can correctly classify parts from the geometric and topological information in 3D CAD models. The test set contains 12 models spanning 10 part classes, with four simple, four moderately complex, and four complex cases. Figure 2 shows representative examples. Simple: screw/bolt Moderate: pulley Complex: crankshaft Figure 2 Part classification examples at different levels of complexity With the names of 10 candidate part classes provided and web search enabled by default, GPT-6 correctly classified all 12 models, achieving 100% accuracy. Mean completion times for simple, moderately complex, and complex cases were 2 min 30 s, 2 min, and 2 min 30 s, respectively. The longest individual test took 4 min. Two additional conditions were tested separately: withholding the candidate class names and disabling web search. Two representative complex cases were selected for each condition, and all were classified correctly. classification error arose when both conditions were applied together: with no candidate class names and web search disabled, GPT-6 misclassified quick-disconnect coupling as check valve (one-way valve), as shown in Figure 3. It identified the internal spring, valve stem, and valve disc, but treated the function of the valve mechanism as the purpose of the coupling as whole. Actual part: quick-disconnect coupling GPT-6 classification: check valve (one-way valve) Figure 3 Misclassification of quick-disconnect coupling In summary, current capabilities and limitations are: For typical parts, GPT-6 can identify both the general part type and the specific type, as well as the part's intended use. For parts with atypical shapes or shapes resembling those of other part types, GPT-6 can identify the general type correctly but may still get the specific type wrong. For assemblies, GPT-6 may mistake the function of one structure within the assembly for the purpose of the whole assembly and assign the wrong part type. B. Feature recognition This task tests whether GPT-6 can identify individual machining features in B-rep model and recognize the relationships between them. It must identify both the general feature type and more specific forms, such as through holes and blind holes, without list of candidate feature types. The test set contains two simple, two moderately complex, and two complex models. Figure 4 shows representative examples.

In two others, GPT-6 identified the actual features correctly but also labeled some groups of faces as features when they were not. In the remaining case, most features were recognized correctly, with small number of errors. Mean completion times for simple, moderately complex, and complex cases were 30 min 30 s, 40 min 30 s, and 1 25 min, respectively. The longest individual test took 2 1 min. Results for the same model were similar with web search enabled and disabled. Each condition gave better results for some distinctions, such as whether holes were through or blind. recurring error was to label groups of faces that did not constitute machining features as features, producing false positives. In complex models, GPT-6 also treated two separate circular holes as single feature and mistook an external cylindrical surface for hole (Figure 5).

sections.content: Figure 5 Errors in distinguishing feature instances and identifying feature types in complex models In summary, current capabilities and limitations are: When features are independent or have only simple nesting relationships, GPT-6 can correctly recognize all machining features, including holes, slots, pockets, and fillets. When features are nested at multiple levels, intersect, or are truncated, GPT-6 can recognize most machining features but still makes some errors. In models with complex overall shapes, it may identify groups of faces as features when they are not. It also has difficulty recognizing internal features when the geometry is densely packed and internal structures are largely hidden from view. C. CAD generation from engineering drawings This task evaluates whether GPT-6 can combine information from multiple views, section views, and dimension annotations to reconstruct the 3D geometry of parts, while ensuring that separately generated parts meet the assembly requirements. The test set contains five single-part cases and three cases involving multiple parts. Two cases are simple, three are moderately complex, and three are complex. Figure 6 shows representative reference models.

sections.title: Complex
sections.content: Figure 6 Examples for CAD reconstruction from engineering drawings at different levels of complexity All parts passed the solid validity checks in six of the eight cases. The other two cases failed because of defects such as self-intersections and non-manifold connections. Of the three cases involving multiple parts, one could be assembled successfully, one had interference between components, and one could not be assembled because of missing structures and incorrect dimensions. Mean completion times for simple, moderately complex, and complex cases were 26 min 30 s, 43 min 40 s, and 31 min 20 s, respectively. The longest individual test took 1 8 min. Typical errors involved inaccurate reconstruction of local structures and incorrect parameters at mating interfaces. In assemblies, the resulting mismatches in mating dimensions caused problems such as overlapping solid bodies (Figure 7).

sections.content: Figure 7 Dovetail profile reconstruction errors and assembly interference In summary, current capabilities and limitations are: GPT-6 recovers the main geometry reasonably well when the relationships among drawing views are clear and the part primarily contains conventional holes, slots, and regular patterns. For parts with multiple steps, nested pockets, or complex transitions in thin walls, however, it remains prone to misinterpreting the structural arrangement and omitting local features. Invalid solids also occur in some cases. For assemblies with few parts and clearly specified mating relationships, GPT-6 can generate part models that fit together. When an assembly has more parts and more complex mating requirements, it struggles to reproduce critical mating dimensions accurately, leading to interference or preventing assembly altogether. In some complex cases, GPT-6 approximates geometry that would conventionally be modeled using draft, shell, or loft operations with basic extrusions and cuts. These approximations do not consistently preserve the required local geometry. D. CAD generation from text This task tests whether GPT-6 can develop design, determine its dimensions, and generate CAD model from geometric or functional requirements. The test set contains four simple, four moderately complex, and four complex cases. Two additional complex assemblies were used for stress testing, and four complex cases were also tested with web search disabled. These are separate outcomes: full requirement score does not establish complete engineering functionality. Mean completion times for simple, moderately complex, and complex cases were 42 min, 1 0 min 15 s, and 1 37 min 30 s, respectively. The longest test took 3 17 min. Of the two stress-test cases, one received full requirement score, but neither passed the solid validity checks. In the four cases tested with web search disabled, all four received full requirement scores, and two passed the validity checks.

sections.content: Figure 9 Typical errors in CAD generation from text In summary, current capabilities and limitations are: For parts with clearly specified dimensions and feature positions, or mechanisms with clear load, motion, and mounting requirements, GPT-6 can develop design from the text, determine its dimensions, and generate individual part models or assemblies. During iteration, it can add missing features and adjust component positions. The mean number of iterations across the 12 cases was four. For models requiring continuous surface transitions or coordinated motion between components, GPT-6 may leave gaps where parts should join, or leave drive components unsecured or disconnected so that motion cannot be transmitted. It also generates unnecessary components with no functional purpose. These errors indicate limitations in its understanding of how components fit together and what they are intended to do. Engineering requirements implicit in the text are therefore not reliably met. For parts with thin walls, intersecting internal holes and cavities, and hole walls close to the outer surface, GPT-6 cannot yet reliably handle surface geometry and the boundaries between adjacent faces. The generated models can contain selfintersections and non-manifold connections. E. CAD reconstruction from rendered images This task uses rendered views without dimension annotations to evaluate whether GPT-6 can recover 3D shape, feature positions, and connectivity. The test set contains two simple, two moderately complex, and two complex cases, with an additional complex housing used for stress testing. Tests also varied the combination of input views and included conditions with web search disabled. Figure 10 shows representative examples.

sections.title: Complex
sections.content: Figure 10 Examples for CAD reconstruction from images at different levels of complexity All 21 test runs produced STEP models, and every solid in the outputs passed the solid validity checks. Across all 21 test runs, mean completion times for simple, moderately complex, and complex cases were 12 min 30 s, 16 min 20 s, and 43 min, respectively. For the six cases tested using six orthographic views and one axonometric view, the mean silhouette intersection over union (IoU) across views ranged from 0.8790 to 0.9915 (Table IV). GPT-6 recovered the main shape and component layout reasonably well, but local structures and absolute dimensions still showed substantial discrepancies. For parts with freeform surfaces, thin walls, and intersecting ribs, GPT-6 often simplifies complex surfaces into planar faces or segmented surfaces and misinterprets feature orientations and connections. For example, the reconstructed control arm in Figure 11 retains the overall outline, but its smooth sidewall surfaces are replaced by segmented surfaces, the root fillets are missing, and local steps are introduced. When the reference model consists of single solid, GPT-6 sometimes produces multiple interpenetrating solids with overlapping volumes. Their connections do not match those of the reference part.

sections.title: Complex
sections.content: Figure 12 Examples for parametric reconstruction from B-rep models at different levels of complexity All 11 cases produced parametric models in SOLIDWORKS format. Six models (54.5% of the total: five simple and one moderately complex) passed the solid validity checks and were therefore eligible for parameter-editing tests. The remaining two moderately complex models and three complex models contained invalid solids. They were excluded from parameterediting tests because they failed the validity prerequisite; their behavior under editing was not tested. Each of the six eligible models underwent 10 single-parameter edits, with only one dimensional parameter changed at time. An edit passed if the parameter change took effect, dependent geometry updated correctly, the edited model passed the solid validity checks, and the model could be restored to its original state. Of the 60 edits, 52 passed (86.7%). Four models passed all 10 edits, accounting for 36.4% of all 11 cases: three simple models and one moderately complex model. Mean completion times for simple, moderately complex, and complex cases were 7 min 36 s, 13 min 20 s, and 50 min, respectively. The longest individual test took 1 52 min. None of the three models tested with web search disabled passed the solid validity checks. The reconstructed models contained sketches, features, and dimensional parameters and resembled the reference shapes, yet incomplete parameter dependencies limited their editability. In one case, increasing the housing depth did not correctly update the dependent hole features, and newly added material closed the existing hole openings. For models with complex surfaces, GPT-6 often uses series of extrusions to approximate the original surfaces with planar faces. Smooth surfaces become densely segmented and stepped, producing large geometric errors. The resulting feature structure is inconsistent with conventional modeling practice for such parts (Figure 13).

sections.title: Reference CAD model
sections.content: GPT-6 reconstruction Figure 13 GPT-6 approximates curved surfaces with planar faces from multiple extrusions In summary, current capabilities and limitations are: For models built mainly from conventional features such as extrusions, revolved features, holes, and slots, with relatively simple dimensional relationships, GPT-6 can reconstruct the main geometry with reasonable accuracy and support some dimensional changes. When hole and slot features depend on the main body dimensions, GPT-6 may fail to establish all the necessary feature dependencies. Changing the main body dimensions can then close hole openings or cause mounting holes to disappear. For models with complex surfaces, GPT-6 often uses series of extrusions to approximate the original curved surfaces with planar faces. Surfaces that are smooth in the reference become segmented and stepped, resulting in large reconstruction errors. IV. Cross-Task Analysis (1) GPT-6 demonstrates capabilities across several kinds of CAD tasks GPT-6 can classify parts and recognize geometric and machining features in existing B-rep models, and generate 3D models from engineering drawings, images, or text descriptions. In some tasks, it can also select design concept from functional requirements, determine dimensions, and perform engineering analyses and checks. The tests include successful cases of feature recognition in relatively complex parts, generation and reconstruction of moderately complex models, and construction of relatively complex assemblies. (2) Generated models do not always form valid solids or meet functional requirements Most generated CAD models resemble the required shape, but errors can remain in their internal structures, critical dimensions, and feature layouts. These errors occur in both individual parts and assemblies: internal passages may not connect or remain separate as required, and components may lack the connections needed to secure them or transmit motion. Some errors have little effect on appearance but directly compromise essential functions. Shape complexity and incomplete input information do not fully explain these failures. Errors also occur in simple models, and even complete information about the target geometry does not guarantee correct reconstruction. (3) Creating 3D model does not guarantee that parametric edits will work correctly For models with simple shapes, few features, and straightforward dependencies, GPT-6 can already create editable parametric models that support dimensional changes and the corresponding updates to dependent features. Even some geometrically simple models have incomplete feature dependencies, while complex reconstructions frequently contain invalid solids. Changing dimension can close hole opening, remove local feature, or displace component. GPT-6 cannot yet consistently produce parametric models that behave correctly when edited. (4) GPT-6 can check and revise its own models, but cannot yet correct errors consistently During modeling, GPT-6 can inspect its results, identify some problems, and revise the models repeatedly. These revisions contribute to successful outcomes in some complex tasks. Yet the tests show that error often fluctuates over successive iterations, and some changes increase it. GPT-6 is therefore still unreliable at identifying the source of an error, deciding what to modify, and selecting the appropriate operation. Dependencies among geometric features and parameters complicate this process: single change may affect several parts of the geometry and multiple design requirements. GPT-6 does not yet fully identify these dependencies or reliably anticipate and control the consequences of an edit. As result, correcting one problem can introduce new errors. (5) Long modeling times limit practical use GPT-6 often cycles repeatedly through model generation, inspection, and correction, which takes considerable time. Mean completion times for several kinds of modeling and reconstruction tasks were in the tens of minutes. Some complex cases took more than an hour, with the longest taking 3 41 min. These times make it difficult to provide the rapid feedback and frequent revisions needed in design work. Despite progress in modeling performance, practical use remains limited. sections.content: GPT-6 uses feedback to add missing features, adjust dimensions and positions, reduce geometric error, and meet more of the requirements. GPT-6 still struggles to decide what to change and how far those changes should extend. Even after several iterations, models may contain invalid solids, lack required functions, or fail when parameter is edited. Long iterations limit practical use. 13 V. Conclusion This study assessed GPT-6 Astra across CAD model understanding, generation, editing, and autonomous evaluation. The system interpreted geometry, constructed parts and assemblies, and developed designs from functional requirements. These successes indicate emerging practical value in conceptual design and initial modeling for detailed design. Engineering reliability remains limited by errors in connectivity, part mating relationships, and parameter dependencies. Geometric similarity and valid individual solids do not establish functional adequacy or reliable editability. Autonomous refinement corrects some defects but leaves others unresolved and can increase geometric error. Long completion times further constrain practical use. Reliable use requires professional verification of the initial model and its response to modification. Preserving the geometric and functional relationships needed for engineering use, while correcting errors without disrupting those relationships, remains central challenge for CAD agents.

sections.title: 1.1 Evaluation objectives
sections.content: This report systematically evaluates how well OpenAI's GPT-6 can understand and generate CAD models. It examines how performance varies with task complexity, the strategies evident in its execution records, and what it can and cannot do. The findings help assess which CAD tasks GPT-6 is close to handling in practice, where its capabilities still fall short, and which research directions deserve priority. Model understanding: Assess how well GPT-6 understands CAD model's geometry and topology, and what the model represents in engineering terms. Model generation: Assess whether GPT-6 can generate CAD models from engineering text descriptions, and rendered images, and construct plausible parametric drawings, modeling history from an existing CAD model. Analyze the observable steps GPT-6 takes to complete each task and establish what it can and cannot do. Synthesize the test results to assess GPT-6s overall CAD capabilities and identify directions for future research in intelligent CAD.

sections.title: 2.1 Task objectives and evaluation criteria
sections.content: The part classification task tests whether GPT-6 can use the geometry and topology in B-rep model (provided as STEP file) to assign mechanical part to one of predefined set of classes. This follows the conventional formulation of part classification, allowing results to be compared on the same basis. Additional tests use open-ended prompts about the part and its engineering use. These go beyond selecting label: they examine whether GPT-6 can identify the part, explain which geometric and structural features support its judgment, and infer its function and typical uses without fixed list of candidate classes. Table 2-1 summarizes the task. Table 2-1 Part classification task Test element Description Research question Can GPT-6 correctly classify mechanical part from STEP model and, without fixed label set, identify the part, explain the structural evidence, and infer its typical functions and uses? Input B-rep model of mechanical part. Expected output Most likely part class or name, the main evidence for the judgment, typical functions and uses, and any necessary explanation of uncertainty. Evaluation criteria For the standard task, the primary criterion is classification correctness within the supplied label set. For the additional tests, the criteria are whether the proposed class or name is reasonable, whether the geometric and structural evidence is accurate, whether the inferred functions and uses are plausible, and whether uncertainty is recognized appropriately.

sections.title: 2.2.1 Test case selection
sections.content: The test cases were drawn from the TMCAD dataset. All represent real mechanical parts with known classes or names. The selection covers range of part classes and identification difficulties, avoiding test set made up only of parts with highly distinctive overall shapes or single local feature that reveals their class. Difficulty was assessed from how typical the part's overall shape is, how much of its geometry must be considered to identify it, how closely it resembles other part classes, and how directly its geometry and topology reveal its function. Table 2-2 gives the complexity criteria. 5 CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. October 2026 Table 2-2 Complexity criteria for part classification

sections.title: Complex
sections.content: The overall shape and key functional structures are characteristic of the class. The part can be identified reliably from its overall shape or few key structures. Distinctive features clearly separate the part from related classes. Classification requires several local structures and their spatial relationships to be considered together. No single feature is decisive, and the geometry may resemble related classes. The main body, mounting structures, hole layout, and supporting or connecting structures must be considered together. The features that distinguish the class are not readily apparent, or the shape and structure closely resemble other classes. Local structures alone can be misleading. Complex industrial parts, nonstandard parts, parts combining several functions, or parts for which more than one classification is plausible. sections.title: 2.2.2 Test conditions
sections.content: The prompts and model responses reproduced in this chapter are English translations of the Chinese records. Machine-readable class labels and case identifiers are retained; prose labels are formatted consistently for readability.

sections.title: 2.2.2.1 Main experiments
sections.content: The main experiments used the environment specified in Section 1.3 and the same prompt for every case. Following the conventional part classification formulation, the prompt supplied predefined set of classes and asked GPT-6 to select the class of the input B-rep model. The candidate classes remained unchanged; only the input model varied. This allowed performance to be assessed across the three complexity levels. The prompt was: "Which of the following part 7 CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. October 2026 classes does the given STEP model belong to: bearing bracket coupling flange gear nut pulley shaft screw_bolt spring?"

sections.title: 2.2.2.2 Additional experiments
sections.content: Additional experiments on representative complex cases examined the effects of prompt wording and access to web search. Two factors were varied. First, the standard classification prompt was replaced with an open-ended prompt that removed the candidate list and requested an explanation of the identification and typical functions or uses. Second, web search was disabled to test performance without that source of external information. The open-ended prompt was: "Identify the most likely type of part represented by this CAD model. Explain which geometric features support your judgment and what functions or uses this type of part typically has. If the part cannot be identified uniquely, give the most likely class and explain the uncertainty." Combining these two factors gives the three additional test conditions in Table 2-4. Only the prompt and web search setting changed; all other settings matched the main experiments. Each test used separate conversation to prevent information from one condition carrying over to another. sections.title: 2.5 Capabilities and limitations
sections.content: For part classification, GPT-6 can query the CAD kernel and inspect model views as needed, combining evidence from the overall shape, local geometric features, and assembly components. It classified every case correctly in the main experiments with predefined classes. Its ability is not limited to parts with typical shapes: when part has an unusual form or resembles another class, GPT-6 can consider several structural features together and provide more specific name and explanation of its function. The two additional tests that retained the candidate classes also returned correct classifications with web search disabled. The main difficulty is determining exactly which type of part model represents. When an assembly lacks information about mating components or its installation, GPT-6 sometimes assigns the whole part class based on the structure and function of just one component. When the overall shape and local geometric features do not fully support the same interpretation, it often proposes specific type without being able to confirm that identification reliably. Overall, GPT-6 has been successful at identifying the general class of part, but is less reliable when asked to determine its specific type. The remaining challenge is to connect the geometric evidence accurately to what the part does and which type it belongs to. These results apply to small, selected set of parts. The 100% result measures classification within the supplied candidate list, not unrestricted identification. In PC-10, the output also cites an embedded STEP model name. sections.title: 3.5 Capabilities and limitations
sections.content: For feature recognition, GPT-6 can combine surface parameters, face adjacency, sectioning where needed, and checks of whether geometry lies inside or outside solid to recognize holes, slots, pockets, bosses, and transition features. It can also associate those features with specific Brep faces. When simple features have clearly separate boundaries, GPT-6 can recognize them correctly and identify their local structure and relationships at different levels. For holes, it can distinguish through holes, blind holes with conical bottoms, and stepped holes. For pockets, it can recognize successive levels and use bottom-face positions and connectivity to distinguish individual features. The main limitations occur in complex regions with multiple levels of nesting, intersections, or interrupted boundaries. GPT-6 sometimes combines two spatially separate holes into one feature or mistakes an external cylindrical surface for hole. Even after locating hole, it may fail to use its bottom and openings fully to determine whether it is through or blind. The workflow analysis in Section 3.4 shows that GPT-6 sometimes uses rendered views to help interpret geometry. Where viewpoints are restricted, occlusion is substantial, or local structures are difficult to discern, reliance on image information may contribute to errors in the grouping of feature faces and the identification of feature types. This may be one cause of the errors in local detail. 39 CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. October 2026 Overall, GPT-6 can recognize basic features with reasonable reliability and handle some complex combinations. However, it does not yet consistently identify all machining features in complex models. When boundaries are unclear, features interact, or local structures are difficult to interpret from model views, it is more likely to merge several features into one or leave their specific types unresolved. sections.title: 4.5 Capabilities and limitations
sections.content: GPT-6 can combine projections across multiple views, section views, dimensions, and relationships between local features to reconstruct the main three-dimensional structures of parts from engineering drawings. For simple and moderately complex cases, it generally reproduces the main outlines, holes and slots, repeated patterns, and most internal structures correctly. For complex individual parts such as the engine block, it can also identify the main hole layouts, cavities, reinforcing structures, and their spatial relationships. When several parts are involved, their correspondence and assembly GPT-6 can model relationships. The moderately complex case can be assembled as intended, and the main components and overall structures of complex assemblies are also reproduced to substantial extent. them individually and interpret The main limitations concern interpretation of complex local geometry, recovery of dimensions, and consistency at assembly interfaces. GPT-6 is prone to simplifying geometry, omitting features, or introducing local topological errors when interpreting multiple steps, nested cavities, holes opening into cavities, through and blind holes, and transitions such as chamfers and fillets. Some models have broadly correct overall shapes but inaccurate depths, wall thicknesses, hole positions, and mating dimensions. In an individual part, these appear mainly as dimensional errors. Across several parts, they can accumulate into interference, mating surfaces that fail to meet, or missing assembly interfaces where essential holes have been omitted. Complex cases 65 CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. October 2026 also contain invalid face intersections, non-manifold geometry, and outputs with no valid solid. GPT-6 therefore cannot yet consistently ensure the validity of complex CAD geometry, or reliably detect and correct local errors and assembly interference. In some complex cases, GPT-6 also uses higher-level CAD operations such as shelling, applying draft, and lofting inconsistently. thin walls, variable cross-sections, and complex transitions that should be formed with these operations are approximated using basic extrusions and cuts. Such approximations can recover the overall shape to some extent, but do not accurately preserve wall thickness, surface transitions, or local assembly interfaces, resulting in distorted or missing structures. This may reflect an incomplete understanding of higher-level CAD features and their engineering purpose, or may be related to the CAD modeling tools used. Overall, GPT-6 shows strong ability to interpret multiple drawing views and reconstruct threedimensional CAD models, but remains well short of reliable engineering use. It can often establish the general shape of part. The remaining challenge is to reconstruct complex local structures accurately, choose appropriate 3D modeling representations, satisfy dimensional and mating requirements, and produce geometrically valid models whose parts assemble consistently. 66 CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. sections.title: 5.1 Task objectives and evaluation criteria
sections.content: CAD generation from text comprises two tasks: modeling from geometric requirements and modeling from functional requirements. The first takes textual description of the target shape, dimensions, quantities, and spatial relationships. It tests whether GPT-6 can interpret these requirements, plan modeling sequence independently, and use CAD software APIs to generate the corresponding B-rep model. The second takes description of the intended application, functional objectives, operating conditions, interfaces, and space constraints. It tests whether GPT-6 can select structural design, determine its parameters, and produce CAD model that meets those needs. Web search is enabled in the main experiments. Additional experiments comprise stress tests for both tasks and tests with web search disabled. These examine GPT-6s ability to handle more complex tasks and to model from the supplied text without web search. Table 5-1 sets out the objectives and evaluation criteria. Table 5-1 Objectives and evaluation criteria for CAD generation from text Test element Description Evaluation question Can GPT-6 generate CAD models whose shapes, dimensions, and spatial relationships match geometric requirements? Can it use functional requirements to select suitable structure and parameters, then generate CAD model that meets the design requirements? Input Output English text describing geometric or functional requirements. Geometric requirements specify target shapes, dimensions, quantities, and spatial relationships; functional requirements specify the intended application, objectives, operating conditions, interfaces, and constraints. B-rep model generated from the input text and delivered as STEP file. single-solid part should be valid solid; an assembly should retain its individual parts and their assembly relationships.

sections.title: 5.2.1 Test case selection
sections.content: Each task includes simple, moderate, and complex cases, with one single-solid part and one assembly at each level, giving 12 cases in the main experiments. Complexity is assessed from the structures specified in the input and the difficulty of designing and modeling them. For geometric requirements, the main challenges are constructing the shapes and resolving spatial relationships 67 CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. sections.title: 5.2.1.1 Cases with geometric requirements
sections.content: For modeling from geometric requirements, complexity depends on the regularity of the geometry, the difficulty of constructing surfaces and internal passages, and the complexity of component positions and connections. Single-solid parts are assessed primarily by the connections and transitions between local features and the main body. Assemblies are assessed by how parts fit together, how mechanisms are connected, and how the assembly is arranged. Table 5-2 defines the criteria. sections.title: Typical characteristics
sections.content: Simple Predominantly constant cross-sections, symmetry, or repeated structures, with little interaction between local features; assemblies consist mainly of one simple mechanism. Regular main shape, few holes or slots, and symmetric or repeated structures; straightforward positioning and connections between parts. Moderate Twisted surfaces or continuous transitions, or mechanism with several interconnected transmission elements. Curved or twisted surfaces and local connections requiring smooth transitions; several parts transmit motion together through gears or linkages. Complex Closely packed internal cavities and passages, with interdependent wall and passage positions; assemblies contain several kinds of components and mechanisms whose spatial arrangements affect one another. Passages in several directions, closely packed cavities, and complex local wall thicknesses and connections; several mechanisms share limited space and require coordinated positioning. The six cases are an electronics heat sink body, push-pull toggle clamp, an impeller with curved blades, VEX robot gripper, Rover V8 engine block, and horizontal single-cylinder steam engine. The reference models are publicly available mechanical models from GrabCAD. The inputs are English geometric requirements written from these reference models, specifying target dimensions, shapes, quantities, and relative positions. sections.content: This section first presents the main results for modeling from geometric and functional requirements, then the additional stress tests and tests with web search disabled. All experiments assess whether the models meet the input requirements and pass the solid validity check. sections.title: 5.5 Capabilities and limitations
sections.content: In this chapters text-to-CAD tests, GPT-6 converts descriptions of geometry and intended use into structural designs. It independently determines dimensions and component relationships, plans the modeling sequence, and uses CAD tools to generate individual parts and assemblies. It can construct repeated features, complex surfaces, and internal passages, and arrange and assemble several mechanisms. During modeling, GPT-6 also uses load and motion calculations and geometric checks to revise structures and parameters, add omitted features, and correct some interference, progressively increasing the proportion of input requirements met. Limitations remain in local detail and implicit engineering requirements. Some models satisfy the explicitly listed shape, dimensional, or layout requirements but have incomplete transitions, fastenings, or transmission connections, or contain unnecessary structures with no practical purpose. These defects affect how components fit together and function. In complex assemblies, some generated parts also contain geometric and topological defects, including self-intersections, non-manifold connections, and open shells, which cause the models to fail the solid validity check. GPT-6 cannot yet reliably detect and correct these problems on its own. It struggles to ensure sound structural details, working mechanisms, and valid solids simultaneously, leaving substantial gap between its outputs and models suitable for engineering use. 103 CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. October 2026 Chapter 6 CAD reconstruction from images

sections.title: 6.1 Task objectives and evaluation criteria
sections.content: This task evaluates GPT-6s ability to interpret renderings from multiple viewpoints and reconstruct three-dimensional CAD model. The main experiment uses consistent set of views and simple Chinese prompt so that reconstruction results can be compared. The main experiment tests six cases using six orthographic views and one axonometric view. The same six cases are also tested with three orthographic views and with six orthographic views alone. Two complex cases are retested with web search disabled, and seventh case is used for stress test, giving 21 runs in total. These comparisons examine how view availability and search access relate to reconstruction quality. Table 6-1 Objectives and evaluation criteria for CAD reconstruction from images Test element Description Evaluation question Can GPT-6 reconstruct CAD model consistent with renderings from multiple viewpoints? How does reconstruction quality change when fewer views are supplied? Input Renderings from multiple viewpoints Output readable B-rep model Evaluation criteria Check solid validity and assess geometric agreement using silhouette IoU, HD between three-dimensional surfaces, and model comparisons. Geometric agreement is assessed in two ways: by comparing view silhouettes and by comparing three-dimensional surfaces. The reference STEP files are used only to check the generated results. Silhouette intersection over union (IoU) measures the overlap between projections of the generated model and the input renderings. Hausdorff distance (HD), in millimeters, estimates the maximum surface deviation between the generated and reference models; smaller value indicates smaller sampled deviation. To calculate HD, the nearest distance from each sampled reference point to the generated point cloud is found, and the calculation is then repeated in the reverse direction. The largest distance across both directions is reported as HD. All models are declared to use millimeters. Points are sampled in proportion to surface area, and the models are rigidly aligned using multiple initial poses and bidirectional iterative closest point (ICP) registration. Alignment permits rotation and translation only, with no scaling or mirroring. Each model uses 12,000 points for registration and separate set of 180,000 points for HD evaluation. All evaluation points are retained. The reported HD is therefore the symmetric Hausdorff distance between finite sampled point clouds, not an exact distance between continuous B-rep surfaces. Because alignment excludes scaling, it reflects differences in absolute scale as well as local shape. Without dimensional cue in the input images, absolute scale is not uniquely recoverable; HD should be interpreted with that limitation in mind. 104 CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. October

sections.title: 6.2.1 Test case selection
sections.content: The cases are publicly available mechanical parts and assemblies. Selection favors representative structures with corresponding STEP reference files. To cover range of modeling difficulties, the cases vary in structural complexity, local feature types, and number of parts. They include sheetlike parts, housings, supports with holes, brackets with curved surfaces, and chassis assembly, covering both single-part and assembly modeling. With the number of input views held constant, complexity is classified primarily by the geometry, spatial relationships between local features, and degree of occlusion. For assemblies, the number of parts and their assembly relationships are also considered. Table 6-2 defines the criteria. Table 6-2 Complexity criteria for CAD reconstruction from images Complexity Selection criteria Typical characteristics Simple The main shape is regular, with few local features. Major outlines, holes, slots, and bosses can be matched clearly across views, with few complex surfaces or occluded structures. Clear outlines and few local features reveal the overall structure, requiring little crossview matching or inference of local shapes. Moderate Complex More local detail and spatial relationships are present, including holes in different directions, inclined connections, or varying cross-sections. Multiple views are needed to determine feature shapes, orientations, and connections, although the main structure remains regular. The renderings contain dense structural detail, including complex surfaces, thin walls, and intersecting features, with some regions occluded. Overall outlines and repetition alone do not reveal local shapes. Assemblies also contain many components and connections that must be interpreted in relation to other parts. Local shapes and positions must be inferred from several views. Clear geometric regularities, repeated features, or welldefined connections can still guide modeling. Geometry distributed across views must be combined to resolve surface variations, structural layers, and connection transitions. In assemblies, local structures must also be interpreted through the positions and correspondence of parts; occlusion adds difficulty. The main experiment comprises six cases: five single parts and one assembly, with two cases at each of the simple, moderate, and complex levels. sections.title: 6.5 Capabilities and limitations
sections.content: In CAD reconstruction from images, GPT-6 can combine silhouettes, holes and slots, and relative positions across multiple views to reconstruct the main structure of part and produce STEP 149 CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. October 2026 model. In these tests, the overall shapes of regular plates and housings were usually recovered. Complex brackets, the chassis, and the bell housing also retained their main components and overall layouts. The main limitations concern freeform surfaces, connections between solids, and dimensions that affect function. Complex freeform surfaces and transitions at rib intersections are often approximated by planes, ruled surfaces, or regular ribs, leaving local curvature, cross-sections, and fillets inaccurate. Some nominally single parts consist of separate solids that overlap at connections without Boolean union. Validity of each solid does not establish that the overall connections are correct. Differences in holes, slots, clips, guides, and assembly interfaces may affect positioning, installation, or load bearing; assumed scales in the absence of dimensional cues may also affect fit. In the two cases tested with web search disabled, models were still generated, but local structures were more simplified than in their corresponding main-experiment results. These comparisons do not establish general effect of web search. CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. October 2026 Chapter 7 Parametric reconstruction from B-rep models

sections.title: 7.1 Task objectives and evaluation criteria
sections.content: This task evaluates whether GPT-6 can infer plausible set of features, sketches, reference geometry, modeling history, and dependencies from the geometry and topology of B-rep model, then reconstruct corresponding parametric CAD model. It tests the combined ability to work backward from final geometry to modeling logic, plan parametric modeling sequence, and execute it. B-rep model can result from several different, equally reasonable parametric modeling histories. An exact node-by-node match to the original feature tree is therefore not required for success. The evaluation separately considers the correctness of the final geometry, the suitability of the parametric structure, reliability under editing, and consistency between the reconstructed modeling history and the input B-rep model. Table 7-1 summarizes the task. Table 7-1 Objectives and evaluation criteria for parametric reconstruction from B-rep models Test element Description Evaluation question Can GPT-6 infer appropriate features, sketches, reference geometry, modeling sequence, and dependencies from B-rep model, then reconstruct geometrically consistent, editable parametric CAD model? Input B-rep model of mechanical part. Output An editable parametric CAD model that matches the input B-rep geometry within the specified tolerance, with an appropriate feature tree, sketches, reference geometry, dimensional parameters, and feature dependencies. Explain the modeling approach and any uncertainty where necessary. Evaluation criteria First assess whether parametric model is produced and how closely its final geometry matches the input B-rep. Then assess the suitability of its parametric structure and reliability under editing.

sections.content: GPT-6 uses the SOLIDWORKS API to produce native project files containing sketches, dimensional parameters, and modeling operations. This section first summarizes all 11 cases, then compares reference and reconstructed models from the same viewpoint. sections.title: 7.3.1.1 Overview
sections.content: All 11 cases use the prompt specified in Section 7.2.2. Geometric agreement is measured by bidirectional root-mean-square (RMS) surface distance. The reference and reconstructed models are first triangulated. Points are sampled uniformly over each meshs surface, allocating samples in proportion to triangle area. The nearest distance from each point to the other mesh is then calculated. lower RMS value indicates closer overall agreement between the surfaces. Reconstructed models are first checked for solid validity. Models that fail this check are excluded from parameter-editing tests and are reported as Not tested (invalid solids). This designation records failure of the validity prerequisite, not an observed editing failure. Each model that passes undergoes 10 single-parameter edits in SOLIDWORKS. In each test, only one dimensional parameter is actively changed; all other input parameters remain fixed, while dependent features update through the existing relationships. The original value is restored after each test. An edit passes only if it takes effect, the model rebuilds successfully, the geometry changes as intended, dependent structures update correctly, the edited model passes the solid validity checks, and the original state can be restored. Hole closure, damage to the geometry, or misalignment of components constitutes failure. Table 7-4 presents the results. sections.title: 7.5 Capabilities and limitations
sections.content: In these tests, GPT-6 can read the geometry and topology of an input B-rep model, create sketches and dimensional parameters, build features such as extrusions, revolves, and cuts, and 173 CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. October 2026 produce editable parts and assemblies. It recovers the main shapes of the three-arm flanged shaft, connecting rod, and pulley support assembly. Iterative modeling also reduces overall geometric error for the pump housing, forked shaft, and complex housings. However, reconstruction of complex surfaces and establishment of parameter dependencies remain incomplete. Some models approximate continuous surfaces by dividing them into cross-sections and stacking simple surfaces. The gearbox cover consequently has densely segmented exterior, and the engine blocks passage profiles are not fully recovered. Parameter edits also expose missing dependencies between features. Only six of the 11 models pass the solid validity check and qualify for editing tests: five simple and one moderate. Each undergoes 10 single-parameter edits, of which 52 pass in total. Only four models pass all 10 editsthree simple and one moderate representing 36.4% of all 11 cases. Increasing the depth of the B2P-03 flanged housing closes hole opening. In another test, reducing flange diameter causes mounting holes to disappear. These failures show that dependent features do not update correctly when the main dimensions change. GPT-6 can construct native parametric models from B-rep inputs and edit some dimensions, but it cannot yet reliably reconstruct both complex surfaces and assembly relationships correctly. Some reconstructed solids fail validity checks, and the chuck also contains faces not belonging to any solid. With web search disabled, complex surfaces are still approximated by layers of simple surfaces. The three comparison cases are insufficient to establish an effect of web search on reconstruction quality. These tests primarily cover single-parameter edits; combinations of parameter changes, feature addition or deletion, and full assembly functionality have not been evaluated. CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. October 2026 Chapter 8 Conclusions The preceding chapters evaluate GPT-6 across six kinds of CAD tasks, from part classification and feature recognition to model generation and parametric reconstruction. This chapter draws together the evidence on the capabilities demonstrated, the requirements that remain difficult to satisfy, and the contribution and limitations of iterative, tool-assisted workflows. The classification and feature-recognition results show that GPT-6 can combine specific geometric information with mechanical-design knowledge to interpret CAD models. For example, it identifies four-throw crankshaft from the connections between its offset shaft sections and crank webs, and double torsion spring from the arrangement of its coils and arms (PC-11 and PC-12). In the bearing case, it identifies the broad class as roller bearing, but also notes that the main roller surfaces are cylindrical and uses this observation to assess whether the model represents standard tapered roller bearing (PC-09). GPT-6 can also distinguish local features and identify relationships between them: in FR-04, it correctly identifies nested pockets at multiple levels, intersecting passages, and mounting holes interrupted by those passages. These results show that GPT-6 can combine geometry, mechanical-design knowledge, and retrieved information to classify parts, recognize features, and explain the basis for its judgments. Correct recognition of local geometry does not, however, ensure correct interpretation of parts overall purpose. In the PC-10 test with neither candidate-class hints nor web search, GPT-6 recognizes the spring and valve stem but classifies the pipe coupling as check valve, mistaking the function of its internal valve mechanism for the purpose of the entire coupling. Feature grouping can fail in similar way. In FR-06, two spatially separate sections of hole wall are grouped as one hole, while an external cylindrical face is incorrectly identified as hole. GPT-6 can use geometry to reason about model, but it still makes mistakes about which faces belong to one feature and what role local feature plays in the whole part. Successful generation cases include solids with complex internal passages and assemblies containing several parts. Given detailed geometric requirements, GPT-6 produces TC-05 as single valid V8 engine-block solid, with connected water jacket isolated from the cylinder bores. In TC-06, it models and assembles the main drive and valve gear of horizontal single-cylinder steam engine. The components and relative positions of the piston rod, crosshead, crank and connecting rod, and eccentric valve gear meet the requirements. These results show that GPT-6 can construct complex internal geometry and position and assemble multiple parts when geometric requirements are specified. Modeling from functional requirements further demonstrates GPT-6s ability to develop design from set of requirements. In TRC-03, it designs pump casing around specified impeller, creating connected flow passages, pipe interfaces, and rear opening for disassembly. It provides clearance for fastening tools and rotor removal and calculates head loss and pressure-bearing capacity for the specified operating conditions. For the pneumatic two-finger gripper in TRC-04, GPT-6 selects parallel-gripping design driven by pneumatic cylinder, synchronized by rackand-pinion mechanism, and guided by shafts that constrain finger motion. Although this differs 175 CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. October 2026 from the reference models linkage mechanism, it meets the functional requirements listed in the test. These tasks involve mechanism selection, interface design, spatial layout, and engineering calculations, showing that GPT-6 can make concrete design choices and implement them in CAD for some tasks. Accurate generation and reconstruction of complex surfaces, thin walls, and local transitions remain recurring difficulties across tasks. D2C-A03 does not accurately recover complex surfaces and thin-walled regions from engineering drawings. In reconstruction from images, I2C-03 approximates the control-arm sidewalls with ruled lofts through multiple sections, leaving the smooth surfaces and root fillets incomplete. In parametric reconstruction from B-rep models, B2P-09 and B2P-10 use extrusions of separate cross-sections to approximate housing surfaces and passage profiles, with substantial geometric deviations or invalid solids. Although the main shape and some holes and slots can be generated, complex surfaces and connection transitions remain difficult to reproduce accurately. Even when the overall shape is present, local passages, the way solids are connected, and assembly relationships may fail to meet the requirements. D2C-P05 produces valid engineblock solid but turns some through holes into blind holes. The control-arm body, bushings, and lug are all present in the three-view I2C-03 result, but the reconstruction consists of separate solids that overlap locally and does not reproduce the reference part as one connected solid. The gripper in TC-04 includes motor, gears, and the associated mechanism parts, yet radial clearance remains between the motor shaft and the pinions central bore, with no set screw or other fastening feature to secure them. The connection therefore cannot reliably transmit torque. Similar problems occur in the helicopter modeled from functional requirements: in TRC-07, the pitch links are not connected to the swashplate, and the gimbal motor is not secured to its support plate. These small geometric errors directly affect function. GPT-6 can thus create quite complex geometry and component layouts while still overlooking local requirements that determine whether the design works. Insufficient input information cannot explain all these failures. Missing scale information in images and internal structures not fully shown in three orthographic views do limit geometric recovery. Yet the STEP files supplied for parametric reconstruction already contain the complete geometry, and the reconstructed models still show substantial approximation. B2P-09 and B2P10, for example, approximate housing surfaces and passage profiles with extrusions of separate cross-sections, leaving large geometric deviations or multiple invalid solids. Five of the 11 parametric reconstructions fail the solid validity check. Complete geometric information must still be extracted, analyzed, and translated into suitable modeling features and operations to produce an accurate reconstruction. These tests show that, even with complete target geometry, GPT-6 cannot yet make full use of that information to reconstruct complex models accurately. Parametric reconstruction exposes further limitations when design is modified. The initial B2P03 flanged housing is valid solid, with bidirectional RMS surface distance of approximately 0.05565 mm. Parameter edits nevertheless cause failures: increasing the side-housing depth from 36 to 54 mm closes an existing hole opening, while other edits remove mounting holes or 176 CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. October 2026 counterbore shoulders or cause dependent features to fail during rebuilding. B-rep describes the models shape but does not uniquely determine the feature history or which dimensions and parts should update together when an edit is made. The tests show that GPT-6 cannot generally ensure the intended behavior under subsequent parameter edits. These capabilities and limitations also need to be understood in terms of how GPT-6 performs CAD tasks. In most cases in this report, it uses an agent workflow that repeatedly generates model, checks the result, and makes corrections based on feedback. In TC-05, for example, the water jacket initially opens incorrectly into the central cavity and longitudinal passages are closed. Iterative revisions are needed to establish the required connectivity and separation. In TRC-02, adjustments to thrust washers, stops, and jaw-fastening features eliminate local interference between moving parts. These revisions demonstrate that GPT-6 can analyze and correct specific problems in an existing model during iteration. Correcting some problems does not mean that all requirements are met by the end of the process. TC-07 reaches 100% satisfaction of the listed geometric requirements, yet the final model still contains non-manifold connections and self-intersecting surfaces and fails the overall solid validity check. In B2P-08, RMS decreases from 1.1260 to approximately 0.4193 mm, but one solid is invalid and 371 faces belong to no solid, so the model is excluded from parameter-editing tests. The effectiveness of iterative improvement must therefore be assessed against each requirement separately; improvement in one metric is insufficient to establish that the task is complete. Some error curves also fluctuate during iteration, showing that edits do not always yield the intended improvement. This suggests that AI models still struggle to identify the source of an error, decide what needs changing, and select the appropriate operation. Moreover, CAD features and parameters are interdependent: one edit can affect several design requirements and introduce new deviations while correcting the original problem. Effective iteration therefore requires accurate identification of both the geometry to change and the scope of the operation, together with an assessment of the consequences for dependent features and design requirements. Iterative correction also incurs substantial time costs. Many modeling and reconstruction tasks take tens of minutes. Complex text-based modeling cases average 1 37 min 30 s, with one case taking 3 17 min. In reconstruction from images, I2C-06 takes 3 41 min, the longest recorded run in the report. Execution records show that some tasks require repeated construction, checking, and correction before the requirements are progressively met. Even where modeling succeeds, long completion times make it difficult to support the rapid feedback, repeated edits, and comparison of alternatives needed during design. Current systems have demonstrated the ability to complete complex tasks, but the time required remains substantial limit on practical usability. 177 CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. sections.content: CAD generation from text GPT-6 combines multiple views, section views, and dimensions to recover the main shape and internal structure. In some cases, the generated parts can be assembled as intended. GPT-6 builds models from geometric descriptions, selects designs to meet functional requirements, and carries out modeling and engineering calculations. CAD reconstruction from images GPT-6 recovers the main shape, main features, and component layout from images showing multiple views. GPT-6 may recognize the general type of part but still misidentify the specific type. It may also mistake the function of one structure within part for the purpose of the whole part. GPT-6 does not always distinguish individual features or identify their types correctly, especially where features are nested or intersect. GPT-6 can misread how complex structures are arranged and get critical dimensions wrong, leaving out local features or creating interference between assembled components. GPT-6 still makes frequent errors in complex features, passage connectivity, local transitions, and connections that secure parts or transmit motion. The models do not consistently meet functional requirements or pass solid validity checks. GPT-6 often simplifies complex surfaces and local transitions. Connections between solids and assembly interfaces may also be incorrect. Without dimensional reference, absolute scale cannot be determined uniquely from the images. Parametric reconstruction from B-rep models GPT-6 recovers the main geometry of simple and moderately complex models, creates parametric models, and supports some dimensional changes. Reconstructed complex surfaces and internal passages can differ substantially from the originals. GPT-6 often fails to establish the dependencies needed for related features to update correctly after an edit.

Agentic iteration
across tasks
sections.content: GPT-6 uses feedback to add missing features, adjust dimensions and positions, reduce geometric error, and meet more of the requirements. GPT-6 still struggles to decide what to change and how far those changes should extend. Even after several iterations, models may contain invalid solids, lack required functions, or fail when parameter is edited. Long iterations limit practical use. 178 CAD Capabilities of General-Purpose AI Models Zou et al. October 2026 The evidence is limited to the selected cases, the stated system configuration, and the checks performed. Complexity is defined separately for each task, so the levels are not common difficulty scale across chapters. The additional comparisons involve few cases and do not quantify variability across repeated runs. Publicly available source models and embedded STEP metadata may also supply prior information; the tests do not isolate those effects. Feature and geometry checks, calculation-based functional assessments, and single-parameter editing tests establish different aspects of performance and should not be combined into single overall success rate. These results support the use of general-purpose AI as an assistant for producing initial CAD models and exploring design alternatives in the demonstrated task settings. Reliable engineering use still requires verification of geometry, solid validity, functional connections, assembly relationships, and parameter dependencies. The central challenge is to make iterative correction consistent across these requirements while reducing the time needed to reach an acceptable model.
